newsitem.title: USA: U.S. companies eye shedding assets thru spin-offs. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 6/2]
newsitem.headline: U.S. companies eye shedding assets thru spin-offs. [CORRECTED 01:00 GMT 6/2]

text.p: U.S. corporations, seeking to fine tune their mix of business units, have increasingly turned to the spin-off as a method of shedding an unwanted businesses.
Although spin-offs picked up in 1996 from 1995, analysts note the number of spin-off transactions, more than 40 last year, pales in comparison to the number of mergers.
In a spin-off a corporation distributes stock in a unit to people owning shares of the parent.

Barbara Goodstein, analyst at Rothschild Inc, said moves by high profile corporations such as AT&T Corp and ITT Corp to spin off units have attracted attention in board rooms all over the U.S.. "When CEO's of companies of that size say that 'smaller is probably better,' then it gives added credibility to the advice," she said.

Some of the more recent deals attracting attention include PepsiCo Inc's plan to spin off its restaurant chains, American Brands Inc's plan to spin off its U.K.-based tobacco business and Westinghouse Electric Corp's plan to spin off its industrial businesses.
Goodstein said U.S. investors have been wary of tobacco companies and American Brands did not win much investor support when it sold its domestic cigarette business but kept the international unit.
But if the now pending spin-off of the international unit is completed, the remaining American Brands could attract new investors, Goodstein said.
It will still be a collection of disparate businesses from faucets to bourbon to golf balls, but the mix will include some with great promise, the analyst said.

Spin-offs gained greater visiblity in the U.S. after 1986 when a tax change meant the device was the only way for a company to divest itself of assets without incurring a corporate level tax, noted Robert Willens, analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Spin-offs often occur when one corporation buys another but does not want to keep every business line in the acquired company.
"Some of them are the result, as in the case of ATT and NCR Corp, of an ill-advised merger," said Goodstein.
First Data Corp was spun-off from American Express Co as it grew and no longer fit the strategy of the parent company.

In other cases, a company has developed a business in-house and has seen it grow to a point where its potential customers are competitors of the parent company. The spinoff becomes the most efficient way of expanding the business and increasing shareholder value.
Lucent Technologies Inc, another big AT&T spin-off, wanted to sell telephone equipment to regional telephone companies increasingly engaged in competition with AT&T.
PepsiCo wanted to sell fountain cola service to restaurant chains which compete with its Kentucky Fried Chicken, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut restaurants.
"PepsiCo, by spinning off its restaurants, will be able to focus more on snacks and soft drinks where they have had a better track record," said Sam Stovall, sector strategist at Standard & Poor's.

Stovall noted that companies usually go to great lengths to ensure that the unit being spun off is a success. He compared doing a spin-off to a parent sending a child off into the world. The parent usually will go to a lot of trouble to make sure the child is launched successfully.
Sometimes the shares of units that are spun-off come under pressure in the stock market initially.

Cooper Cameron Corp is one that went more or less straight up after being spun out of parent Cooper Industries Inc (corrects from Cooper Tire & Rubber Co ), Goodstein said. Cooper Cameron supplies equipment to the oil and gas industry while the former parent, makes electrical products, tools and hardware and automotive products. Cooper Cameron has risen from a share price of around 18 at the time of the spinoff in July (corrects from April) 1995 to a current price of around 70. Gardner Denver Machinery Inc, also spun out of Cooper Industries (corrects from Cooper Tire), likewise skyrocketed after a spinoff.
Goodstein said the spun-off units often benefit from managements that can bring turnaround expertise combined with industry experience and a long term vision for the newly independent company.

But, she said, if the management style is just to "slash and burn" for the short term the result may well be disappointing. "There's no free lunch and none of these things are risk free," Goodstein said.
